title: SANDERS v HAMILTON CITY COUNCIL
text:
Attention is drawn to
orders prohibiting
publication of certain
information in this
determination
IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY
AUCKLAND
I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI
TᾹMAKI MAKAURAU ROHE
[2026] NZERA 517
3148881
BETWEEN ASHLEIGH SANDERS
Applicant
AND HAMILTON CITY COUNCIL
Respondent
Member of Authority: Nicola Craig
Representatives: Allan Halse, advocate for the applicant
Karina McLuskie, Tom Jarman and Jake Russ, counsel
for the respondent
Investigation Meeting: 5 and 6 December 2023 in Hamilton
Submissions (and further Up to 1 May 2026 from the applicant
information) received: Up to 1 April 2026 from the respondent
Date: 3 August 2026
DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment relationship problem
[1] Ashleigh Sanders was a zookeeper at Hamilton Zoo from 2017 to 2020. The Zoo
is operated by Hamilton City Council (HCC or the Council).
[2] Ms Sanders developed concerns about the Zoo which are on their face quite
multi-faceted – including micromanagement, lack of clarity about processes, lack of
training and development opportunities, too high a workload for staff, animal welfare
issues and discomfort with a senior manager.

[3] Ms Sanders brings unjustifiable disadvantage and unjustified constructive
dismissal grievances to the Authority with the HCC responding that she was not
disadvantaged and was constructively dismissed.
Non-publication orders
[4] Both parties seek non-publication orders.
[5] Ms Sanders pursues an order covering the mental health impacts on her during
and subsequent to her employment with HCC. This application was not opposed.
[6] HCC seeks an order about a report from AUT regarding a staff survey. HCC
asserts that the report was commissioned on a private and confidential basis, with some
aspects containing commercially sensitive information. Further, employees who
participated did so on the basis that their contribution and any results would be
confidential.
[7] The Authority has the power to prohibit publication under clause 12(1) of
Schedule 2 of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act). The principle of open
justice must be the starting point with sufficient grounds established to justify the
displacement of that presumption. Specific risks of harm should be identified then
weighed, with the reasonable likelihood of occurrence, against the open justice
principle.1
[8] Considering the evidence before the Authority, exposure of mental health
impacts on Ms Sanders has the potential to have significant negative impact on her life
and there is a reasonable likelihood of those occurring to her.
[9] Similarly, the possibility of elements of the staff survey causing impact upon
staff who spoke in confidence and future unwillingness to speak, also on disclosure of
the Zoo’s confidential information impacting on it and the Council and its ability to
undertaking such surveys, warrants an order.
[10] In conclusion, except to the extent included in this determination, a permanent
non-publication order is made regarding:
1 MW v Spiga Limited [2024] NZEmpC 147.

(a) Mental health impacts on Ms Sanders during and subsequent to her
employment with HCC; and
(b) The staff survey of Zoo staff conducted by AUT.
Authority’s investigation
[11] Ms Saunders came to the Authority in mid-2021 but she was unable for reasons I
do not need to detail to proceed to an investigation meeting in the usual timeframe. Later
an investigation meeting was held in Hamilton on 5 and 6 December 2023. Evidence was
heard under oath or affirmation in person or by phone from Ms Sanders and three former
co-workers in her support and for HCC, a curator of one section of the Zoo, the former
acting Zoo Director Lee-Ann Jordan and the current Zoo Director Dr Baird Fleming.
Both parties provided witness statements from people who then no longer wished to give
evidence, with their statements then set aside.
[12] Following the meeting the Authority sought additional information, which was
provided where available. Submissions were timetabled but not received in time after
events described below.
[13] From December 2023 circumstances impacted the progression of this matter. Ms
Sanders’ representative Allan Halse lodged an application for summons of information
with the Authority seeking her file from a third party, Joanne (Jo) Thomson, director of a
company Mr Halse had been employed by. This related to difficulties Ms Sanders’
representative Mr Halse expressed about accessing the files regarding this and other cases
which were with the organisation he had been working for, which operated as Hamilton
CultureSafe.
[14] The Authority sought and received submissions from the parties on that
application but concluded that it had the documents necessary for the purposes of its
investigation. Further documents were not sought from Ms Thomson, thus the application
to issue a witness summons for her was declined.
[15] A subsequent suggestion by the Authority of further mediation was declined by
the parties.
[16] The Authority is aware of a subsequent attempt in the Employment Court to
progress provision of these files. That did not appear to assist in this matter however, on

10 March 2026 the Authority was advised that Ms Sanders wished to proceed with this
matter and final submissions were provided on her behalf. Subsequently submissions
from HCC and reply submissions for Ms Sanders were received.
[17] This determination has not recorded all material received from the parties but has
stated findings, expressed conclusions and specified orders made as a result, as permitted
by s 174E of the Act.
Issues
[18] The issues for investigation are:
(a) Did Hamilton City Council act unjustifiably to Ms Sanders’ disadvantage,
including good faith considerations, regarding failure to:
• follow procedures and investigate bullying
• provide a safe working environment and address health and safety
issues
• respond to grievances when raised?
(b) Was Ms Sanders constructively dismissed and if so, also considering
good faith, was that unjustified?
(c) If a grievance is established, what remedies, if any, should Ms Sanders
receive, including lost wages and compensation?
(d) Should any party have to contribute to the costs of another?
Summary of Ms Sanders’ background and work at the Zoo
[19] Ms Sanders has a long interest in animals. She undertakes a Bachelor of Science
degree at Waikato University, majoring in Animal Behaviour. Her personal life has
challenges with unwellness in her extended family.
[20] Ms Sanders first goes to the Zoo on a student placement before becoming a
permanent employee in November 2017. Her work is on a part time basis for several
years, initially 0.4 FTE then 0.9 FTE.2 For her last few months she is full time.
[21] For a year and a half Ms Sanders works in Ungulates (hooved mammals). Then
for a few months she is seconded to the Natives section of the Zoo, before returning to
Ungulates. A few months of secondment to Primates follows. She returns to Ungulates
in March 2020, then is moved to Primates in May that same year.
2 FTE – Full time equivalent.

Difficulties arise
[22] Ms Sanders’ perception is that she is moved around quite a bit, not knowing who
she is reporting to. The Zoo refers to some moves being at her request after she is
dissatisfied regarding her team leader or manager in one team.
[23] Ms Sanders at several points feels concerned about animal treatment and welfare
but finds responses to raising issues about that unsatisfactory and this is distressing for
her.
[24] Other concerns of Ms Sanders and at least some other staff are short-staffing
making it difficult to get leave time unless it is booked several weeks in advance and late
announcement of rosters meaning staff do not necessarily know whether they would be
working the following day. She understandably sees this making work/life balance very
difficult and expresses dissatisfaction verbally.
T’s involvement
[25] Whilst in her student placement a new operations manager role is created, a step
down from the Zoo Director who is in charge of the Zoo. The appointee, referred to here
as T, creates, in Ms Sanders’ view a distinct change in the environment or style of
management. Although it appears there was some initial enthusiasm for T, this view
changes amongst some and a number are dissatisfied. Ms Sanders sees experienced zoo-
keepers leaving over a period.
[26] An example of a change initiated by T is the addition of extra ‘encounter’ sessions
for customers with animals which Ms Sanders sees as adding considerably to the amount
of work for keepers, without any additional staff.
[27] T is someone without previous zoo experience. Ms Sanders has little to do with
him initially when he is the operations manager. Once he becomes the director, she
identifies that he selects people to communicate with in private, including her. He seeks
her out, particularly when she is alone and asks her questions in a way she describes as
“spy like”, creating a “pseudo-safe place” to encourage disclosures.
[28] One of her colleagues described him to the Authority as grooming people he knew
he could control and working to get rid of people he could not control, creating a climate
of fear.

[29] Ms Sanders feels T remembers things told to him and uses them against people.
If people speak up, he regards them as problem people. Ms Sanders describes him
creating an unsafe environment where staff did not know who was watching them or who
was telling on whom. She recalls T asking for private information about people and
rewarding those who provide it with work opportunities if the information was useful. As
a result, staff do not feel safe in the workplace and it divides people rather than bringing
them together. There is some support from other witnesses of this impression of T’s
approach or management style. One of HCC’s witnesses says there are staff expressing
that T operated on favouritism.
[30] After some time, T starts texting Ms Sanders late at night, initially to ask about
work. He calls her, wanting to catch up. She feels this behaviour escalates when Ms
Sanders separates from her boyfriend who also works at the Zoo. She recalls T telling
her things about her ex-boyfriend’s work performance and talking about T’s own life. He
asks her out for coffee once or twice but she turns him down.
[31] Ms Sanders tries to put some space between them after he calls her to his office a
lot. But he still approaches her and she attempts to provide minimal responses.
[32] Not all these events were supported by documentary evidence but I found Ms
Sanders’ evidence on T credible. A few contemporaneous examples are covered below.
[33] There is a 2018 email exchange between Ms Sanders and T on an article about
burnout which she has found and sent through. She refers in the email to a piling up of
zoo jobs which affects her and she believes others too. In reply T expresses some concern
about her perspective when she has just put forward an innovation (proposal) and received
funding for it. He says he is “happy to pull the pin” if it impacts on her core duties.
[34] Ms Sanders messages a co-worker/friend, including that when she asked T how
she was tracking, he tells her that it did not matter how hard she works:
I’ve been told I sabotaged myself for any future opportunities of training or
development because I dated [W]3
[T] said to me in his office when I asked how I was tracking and if I’m going to
be doing any training in the future.
3 W was a fellow zoo employee.

He said it doesn’t matter how hard you work Ash, you’re not going to go
anywhere because you don’t have the relationships.
As well as dating [W], I ruined my chances at the zoo.
[35] Further on 26 June 2019 Ms Sanders emails the same friend:
And I asked [T] where I was going or how I am developing in the future at the
zoo and he started talking about [W] and I and our relationship and I just let him
talk and then I said to him that had nothing to do with what I’m talking about
and he told me I’ve been performing better since I broke up with [W] and I said
no [W] and I have nothing to do with this and that is because I moved off the
ungulate team. Then he told me that I am not gonna be trained or developed
because I got into a relationship with [W] and then I cried because [W] and I
asked the managers for permission to date because our careers came first. And
then he told me because I don’t get along with [K] or [N], I better “kiss ass” to
[Y] and [B] if I want to get trained on anything and I told him about all the shit
with [Z] and [X] and … he said oh well that’s just because they’re the squeaky
wheels and they’re annoying or they’re the favourite so they get what they want
and the people that work hard and do their job just stay in the background.
“Doesn’t matter how hard you work Ash, you’re not going to get anywhere
because the managers don’t like you”. “But I like you Ash, I’ll fight for you,
I’ll push for you to be trained., Our relationship’s really good so yeah that’s
alright”.
Ms Sanders’ concerns
[36] Ms Sanders told the Authority that she expressed her concerns about the work
environment at team meetings to team leaders or 2IC’s.4 She describes this as being more
talking about issues but not about herself. It was difficult to identify the times this occurs,
there were no notes from such meetings presented by either party. Ms Jordan
acknowledges that some of these processes were deferred and delayed by Covid.
[37] At the Authority’s meeting Ms Sanders referred to have sent an email to HCC in
September 2019 outlining her workplace concerns. She did not supply that email and it
was not referred to in her statement of problem or witness statement. Noone else at the
meeting was aware of it and HCC’s searches of its internal systems were unable to locate
it.
[38] Jumping a little ahead to after a subsequent change in management, an HR
business partner based at the Zoo from around mid/late 2019 and is keeping an eye on Ms
Sanders, along with other staff. Ms Jordan says the HR partner was encouraging Ms
4 2IC’s – second in charge.

Sanders to make a formal complaint, which as far as she was aware only related to T’s
conduct. Ms Jordan is not aware of that eventuating.
Union raises questions concerns and HCC takes action
[39] Backtracking, Council HR and health and safety people are aware for some time
of concerns from zoo staff, but according to Ms Jordan there was a lack of specificity
making action challenging. There is evidence from one of Ms Sanders’ co-workers who
had involvement with the Public Service Association (PSA) that staff were too fearful to
come forward.
[40] There is some monitoring of the situation ongoing by Council.
[41] Later culture concerns are raised by the PSA in a more formal manner – including
fatigue, low morale, staff not feeling heard and some bullying allegations. Ms Jordan
accepts there were rostering issues although this was a perennial issue rather than
something specifically related to management before her appointment. The Council
decides to undertake a psychosocial survey through AUT to ensure confidentiality and an
anonymous forum for staff to share their experiences.
[42] Ms Jordan is appointed as interim Zoo Director in September 2019 and makes a
number of changes, some of which are referred to below. Ms Sanders does not really see
positive impacts eventuating from Ms Jordan’s efforts to make changes although wider
staff survey evidence referred to below does point to an improvement at the Zoo.
[43] A staff engagement survey was undertaken and released in 2020 with the Zoo’s
engagement score recording 9% below the HCC overall level and 7% below the
government benchmark. Some more specific categories were up to 25% below the
government benchmark. Ms Jordan accepts that favouritism was a theme, although
fatigue and low morale were assessed as bigger issues. Only 33% of participants believed
action will take place as a result of this survey, substantially less than the Council and
government benchmarks. In the 2021 survey, generally improved results were recorded
compared to 2020, with some factors over overall Council and government benchmarks.
Ms Sanders’ situation
[44] In October 2019 Ms Sanders suffers from a panic attack at work, feeling she was
being expected to be in several places at once. This includes being called several times

on the radio to ask her to do a task and about where she was, when she has been called
into a meeting. She is assisted by the HR business partner for an immediate session with
a counsellor.
[45] Ms Sanders has a number of health appointments over the period from October
2019 to December 2020. She initially reports increasing workplace anxiety and has
several mental health related appointments, including two counselling sessions in March
2020 and three in November/December 2020. Her perception is of counsellors
recommending she leave the zoo and find other work.
[46] Some senior managers have a sense that Ms Sanders’ emotional/mental state was
being affected by her issues going on for her in her personal life, including her break up
with W, flatting difficulties and serious family unwellness. These matters are identified
in her counselling notes, although it is difficult to get a clear picture of whether they are
mentioned as current or past issues.
[47] A senior manager reports to Ms Jordan that Ms Sanders is unsettled and seeking
a change of team. There is a lack of written evidence at this or other times of interactions
where it seems likely Ms Sanders voices dissatisfaction. For example, the curator who
gave evidence recalls speaking to the then operations manager about Ms Sanders’
negative comments but does not know what that manager did in response. There appears
to have been systems for 1 on 1 meetings by team leaders with staff and for regular
performance appraisals but very little documentation has been able to be provided by the
Zoo regarding these interactions with Ms Sanders over the course of her employment. It
may be that the moves between different areas of the Zoo did not assist in this regard.
[48] In early May 2020 Ms Sanders moves on a permanent basis to the primates team.
From Ms Jordan’s perspective things seem to be going very well then Ms Sanders seems
to become unsettled again. Also, like other organisations and people, the Zoo is impacted
by the Covid pandemic.
[49] Dr Baird is appointed, starting on 1 September 2020. He has regular discussions
with Ms Sanders, finding her an exuberant and emotional individual who is vocal about
her opinions. He is open for such discussions, has respect for her work and overall feels
like she was doing pretty well in the September to November 2020 period. He is not
aware of her having mental health issues. Dr Baird does not receive any complaint of
bullying from her about other managers, former or current.

[50] Ms Sanders texts a friend about finding the new director nice and he listens (to
people). She notes that he listened to her more than anyone else at the Zoo had. Ms
Sanders told the Authority that Dr Baird tried to find out what was going on for her but
she was reluctant to detail her concerns after her earlier concerns had been disregarded
(by others).
[51] But, remaining unhappy, Ms Sanders looks for other work, seeking and being
provided with positive reference letters from a team leader and a veterinarian at the Zoo.
Ms Sanders resigns
[52] Ms Sanders describes her mental health as deteriorating in this time. She accepts
that animal welfare concerns are part of that. She refers to not doing well, crying most
days, feeling depressed, with very prevalent anxiety which she had not experienced before
working at the Zoo. It is hard for her to come to terms with her decision to leave, as
animal work is her passion.
[53] Ms Sanders resigns, in her 1 December 2020 email, thanking her relatively new
team leader for his hard work and effort into the team which will benefit them and the
animals but concluding:
Unfortunately, my mental health is severely compromised working here and I
can no longer continue to do so.
[54] The Zoo Director Dr Fleming wishes to talk to Ms Sanders but she was not
comfortable, and it does not end up happening. Then unfortunately during her notice Ms
Sanders breaks her ankle and is unable to work out her notice period.
Events after dismissal
[55] Ms Sanders’ mental health deteriorates after her employment finishes. About 11
months after her resignation, Ms Sanders requires intensive mental health intervention.
A progress note from April 2022, about five months after that intervention, provided to
the Authority, focuses on her then current presentation, which was residual depressive
symptoms with anxiety. The purpose of the report is not primarily to assess whether work
problems caused Ms Sanders’ mental health difficulties - but the report does note that Ms
Snaders is very nervous and ambivalent about resuming work and her personal grievance
case and related events are listed as psychological stressors that may be contributing to
her current mental state.

[56] In 2022 Ms Sanders moves away from Hamilton to live with her grandmother for
a fresh start. She later returns to live in Hamilton by the time the Authority’s meeting
occurs.
Disadvantage grievances
[57] Ms Sanders’ disadvantage grievances focus on arguments that the Council failed
to follow its process by investigating bullying claims, to provide a safe working
environment and to respond to grievances raised.
[58] By way of background the Council’s Management Policy – Harassment, Bullying
and Discrimination defines Harassment as:
Any behaviours directed towards an individual or a group that a reasonable
person, having regard to the circumstances would expect to insult, intimidate,
victimise or disadvantage the recipient that is unwelcome, hurtful or offensive
to the recipient and is repeated, or is of such significance as to adversely affect
the recipient’s employment or wellbeing.
[59] The policy encouraged to talk to the person bullying or harassing them or their
manager or if the complaint involves the manager, then the manager’s manager. A formal
complaint may be lodged with the complainant’s manager or People, Safety and
Wellness. Formal complaints cannot be kept anonymous and will be given to the staff
member who is the subject of the complaint.
[60] Included is the WorkSafe definition of bullying includes reference to “repeated
and unreasonable behaviour directed towards a worker or a group of workers that can lead
to physical or psychological harm”.
[61] HCC’s position is that it did not fail to provide a safe working environment – it
can only respond to concerns it is made aware of but took action when it became aware
of culture concerns it was responsive and took meaningful steps to ensure a safe working
environment at the Zoo.
[62] HCC’s evidence is that in response to Ms Sanders’ and others’ concerns about
staff fatigue and support it took steps including:
• implementing a new roster guaranteeing consecutive days off
• ensuring employee assistance programme (EAP) support available
• engaging PWC to consult and develop a better team and animal run structure

• hired an external consultant to assess its health and safety procedures for certain
animals
• conducted an internal audit of its health and safety procedures
• introduced a new team and run structure, including adding five new keep
positions
• implementing greater procedures about the emotional care aspects of being a
zookeeper, including new emotional debriefing sessions for staff in distressing
situations
• appointing an expert animal trainer to support and coach staff
• changed the number some species of animals held to reduce keeper workload
• regularly undertaking staff engagement surveys to address and alleviate concerns
raised.
[63] In response to Ms Sanders’ concerns about her personal mental health issues HCC
reports providing her with additional one-on-one support, including:
• EAP services and counselling sessions
• informal meetings and daily catch ups with management to monitor her progress
• guiding her through its policies to ensure she felt comfortable raising any
concerns.
[64] HCC also identifies that Ms Sanders was dealing with significant personal
concerns during her employment which contributed to the deterioration of her mental
health, with these being beyond its control.
Disadvantage grievance established regarding T’s behaviour
[65] I have chosen to deal with the first two disadvantage grievances in a somewhat
different way to how they were described before the investigation meeting. Under s 122
of the Act the Authority is able to find a personal grievance of a type other than that
alleged.
[66] Ms Sanders was disadvantaged by unjustifiable actions of T, the Council’s
manager at the zoo workplace.
[67] The behaviour comes very close to amounting to sexual harassment. Ms Sanders
acknowledges there was no explicit sexual element but he did ask her out for coffee and
tell her that their relationship was good so he would fight for her (against more junior
managers under him). There was an insidious element to it. They had an uncomfortable
exchange when he was away once and he said not to email or text or ring when he was

away. At another point he messaged asking her if she missed him, with a winking face
emoji.
[68] There was no apparent legitimate work reason for T to initiate the level of contact
with Ms Sanders which he did, including out of work hours. Ms Sanders told the
Authority that she did not feel safe calling T out by complaining about him. She did
indicate to him that she did not want to talk about her personal life but he persisted.
[69] It is also more likely than not that T sought to make Ms Sanders give him
information about others which he could use against them.
[70] Ms Sanders’ evidence was that she was disadvantaged when she tried to put limits
up on T. For example, another staff member who was appointed at the same time as her
progressed to full time work much more quickly than Ms Sanders did. She reports T told
her she would not be getting full time right now because of her actions in trying not to
engage with him when, in her words, he was trying to spy on people.
[71] Another example was what could be seen as a threat by T to revoke a Council
funded innovation project Ms Sanders had, after she raised issues about staff fatigue. The
team leader of the area she was working in at the time told her she would lose her job first
if she did things like sending the email about fatigue or the team being stressed by
workload.
[72] The Council was aware there were difficulties on the site during T’s time but did
not take steps until it had a firmer foundation on which to proceed.
[73] In conclusion the behaviour by the Zoo’s most senior manager was unacceptable.
Unjustified disadvantage – failure to respond to grievances
[74] Although personal grievance correspondence after Ms Sanders’ resignation
referred to Ms Sanders having raised grievances through her employment, by the time of
the investigation meeting it is no longer suggested that she raised personal grievances
during her employment at the Zoo.
[75] It was confirmed on her behalf at the investigation meeting that this disadvantage
grievance relates to events after Ms Sanders’ employment finished. Her grievance was
raised by 28 March 2021 letter. Employers are encouraged to respond and seek resolution

of grievances raised after employment finishes. But personal grievances relate to events
occurring when an employee is in an employment relationship.
Constructive dismissal
[76] Constructive dismissals usually fall within one of three categories:
• the employer gives the employee a choice between resigning or being dismissed
• the employer undertakes a course of conduct intended to bring about the
employee’s resignation
• the employer breaches its obligations to the employee so seriously as to justify the
employee’s resignation.5
[77] In this case the third category is relied on. For ‘breach of duty’ dismissals the
approach is to examine whether:
• the resignation was caused by the employer’s breach of duty
• and, the breach of duty was of sufficient seriousness to make it reasonably
foreseeable by the employer that the employee would not be prepared to work
conder those conditions – was a substantial risk of resignation reasonably
foreseeable?6
Assessment of constructive dismissal
[78] Ms Sanders resigned in the 1 December 2020 email.
[79] Despite much exploration with Ms Sanders, the Authority was unable to identify
events in the year or so before her resignation which she relies on to establish her
constructive dismissal. She had numerous concerns about T but his employment with
HCC ended in October 2019 and Ms Jordan was in place as acting director from
September 2019.
[80] Not insubstantial support was provided by the HR business partner to Ms Sanders,
after Ms Jordan’s appointment. Ms Jordan is aware of a decline in Ms Sanders in 2020
but also of the business partner’s support along with the counselling provided. Ms Jordan
only knew about Ms Sanders having one panic attack which she was supported through.
The business partner reported to Ms Jordan that Ms Sanders was often reluctant to accept
5 Auckland, etc Shop Employees, etc IUOW v Woolworths (NZ) Ltd [1985] 2 NZLR 372, CA.
6 Auckland Electric Power Board v Auckland provincial District Local Authorities IUOW [1994] 1 ERNZ
168 at 172.

help with Ms Jordan seeing Ms Sanders as a very private person. Ms Jordan’s assessment
is that she and the business partner were doing all they could to address Ms Sanders’
concerns and support her.
[81] Mr Baird started after that and Ms Sanders on contemporaneous evidence found
him nice and good at listening. He tried to explore her concerns but she was reluctant to
share.
[82] As noted above, neither party were able to locate an email from September 2019
about Ms Sanders’ concerns and no witnesses other than her could recall having seen in,
when questioned.
[83] On the evidence before the Authority, it was hard to conclude that Ms Sanders’
unhappiness about how she was treated by T or concerns about the culture under his
command, were the cause of her resignation some 14 months after he left. Her resignation
email is positive about her team leader. She does say that her mental health is severely
compromised after working at the Zoo. In the absence of a solid medical foundation, it
is difficult to conclude that events which occurred in the pre-October 2019 period caused
Ms Sanders to get to the point in December 2020 where she was no longer able to continue
working.
[84] Ultimately it is not established that Ms Sanders’ resignation was caused by
breaches of duty by HCC.
[85] Even if breach or breaches of duty by HCC did cause the resignation, there
remains the question of whether the breach/es were sufficiently serious to make it
reasonably foreseeable by the employer that Ms Sanders would not be to work conder
those conditions – was a substantial risk of resignation reasonably foreseeable?
[86] The evidence just above does not support that. The departure was not sudden with
Ms Sanders seeking references from staff at least a couple of weeks before she handed in
her resignation.
[87] It is not established that Ms Sanders was constructively dismissed and thus her
unjustified dismissal grievance is not successful.

Remedies
[88] Ms Sanders seeks lost wages after her dismissal and compensation for
humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings.
[89] She has established a disadvantage grievance rather than a dismissal and only a
remedy of compensation under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act is applicable.
[90] Ms Sanders describes herself as becoming isolated, with times of intense
discomfort caused by T’s behaviour. She was intrusively asked about her personal life
Ms Saunders had a sense of heading towards a bad outcome but was afraid to report T.
Her dignity and feelings were injured by this behaviour.
[91] In terms of impact on Ms Sanders, one of her colleagues describes seeing Ms
Sanders as an excited, vibrant and bright student becoming withdrawn and fearful of
talking to others. There is also evidence of Ms Sanders’ mental health challenges. It is
somewhat challenging to pare off the elements of effect on Ms Sanders from matters
which do not concern the disadvantage grievance established, from those which do.
However, I conclude that Ms Sanders is entitled to $18,000 compensation for humiliation,
loss of dignity and injury to feelings.
[92] Ms Sanders did not contribute to the situation giving rise to T’s behaviour in a
blameworthy and causative way. No deduction is warranted under s 124 of the Act.
Orders
[93] Within 28 days of the date of this determination Hamilton City Council is ordered
to pay Ashleigh Sanders $18,000 without deduction as compensation for her grievance.
Costs
[94] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs
between themselves.
